source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις θέλων παραστῆσαι ὅτι ἀλγεινὰ καὶ ἀνιαρὰ ἦν τὰ συμβάντα αὐτῷ καὶ ὅτι οὐχ οἷόν τε ἦν βουληθέντα αὐτὸν ποιῆσαι εἶναι αὐτὰ μὴ τοιαῦτα λέγει· τί οὖν ποτνιᾶται καὶ ὀδύρεται καὶ τὸν τοῦ ὀλέθρου φόβον εὔχεται παραδραμεῖν. λέγων ὧδέ πως· „ὦ πάτερ. εἰ δύναται τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο παρελθεῖν;“ καὶ ἐν τούτοις δὲ ὅρα τὸ τοῦ Κέλσου κακοῦργον, ὅτι μὴ ἀποδεξάμενος τὸ φιλάληθες τῶν ἀναγραψάντων τὰ εὐαγγέλια, δυνηθέντων μὲν παρασιωπῆσαι τὰ. ὡς Κέλσος οἴεται. ἔγκλητα οὐ σιωπησάντων δὲ διὰ πολλοὺς λόγους. οὓς ἐν καιρῷ τις ἀποδώσει τὸ εὐαγγέλιον διηγούμενος. κατηγορεῖ τῆς εὐαγγελικῆς λέξεως προσεκτραγῳδῶν καὶ τιθεὶς μὴ τὰ ἀναγεγραμμένα· οὐ γὰρ εὑρίσκεται. πῶς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὀδύρεται. καὶ παραφράζει μὲν τὸ „πάτερ, εἰ δυνατόν ἐστι, παρελθέτω τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο,“ οὐκέτι δὲ καὶ τὸ αὐτόθεν ἐμφαῖνον τὴν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα εὐσέβειαν αὐτοῦ καὶ μεγαλοψυχίαν ἑξῆς δὲ τούτῳ ἀναγεγραμμένον παρατίθεται οὕτως ἔχον· „πλὴν οὐχ ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω. ἀλλ᾿ ὡς σύ.“ ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ τὴν πρὸς τὸ βούλημα τοῦ πατρὸς περὶ τῶν κεκριμένων αὐτὸν παθεῖν εὐπείθειαν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ δηλουμένην ἐν τῷ „εἰ οὐ δύναται τοῦτο παρελθεῖν. ἐὰν μὴ αὐτὸ πίω. γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου“ προσποιεῖται ἀνεγνωκέναι. ὅμοιόν τι ποιῶν τοῖς κακουργότερον ἀκούουσι τῶν θείων γραφῶν ἀσεβέσι καὶ „ἀδικίαν εἰς τὸ ὕψος“ λαλοῦσι. καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖνοι τοῦ μὲν „ἐγὼ ἀποκτενῶ“ δοκοῦσιν ἀκηκοέναι καὶ πολλάκις ἡμῖν αὐτὸ ὀνειδίζουσι. τοῦ δὲ „ζῆν ποιήσω“ οὐδὲ μέμνηνται· τοῦ ὅλου ῥητοῦ δηλοῦντος τοὺς ἐπὶ κοινῷ κακῷ ζῶντας καὶ ἐνεργοῦντας κατὰ κακίαν ἀποκτείννυσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ. ζωὴν δ᾿ αὐτοῖς κρείττονα ἀντεισάγεσθαι καὶ ἣν δῴη ἂν ὁ θεὸς τοῖς τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀποθανοῦσιν. οὕτω δ᾿ ἐκεῖνοι ἤκουσαν μὲν τοῦ „πατάξω“ οὐκέτι δὲ ὁρῶσι τὸ „κἀγὼ ἰάσομαι“· ὅ τι ὅμοιόν ἐστι λεγομένῳ ὑπὸ ἰατροῦ, διελόντος σώματα καὶ τραύματα χαλεπὰ ποιήσαντος ἐπὶ τῷ ἐξελεῖν αὐτῶν τὰ βλάπτοντα καὶ ἐμποδίζοντα τῇ ὑγιείᾳ, καὶ οὐ καταλήξαντος εἰς τοὺς πόνους καὶ τὴν διαίρεσιν ἀλλ᾿ ἀποκαθιστῶντος τῇ θεραπείᾳ τὸ σῶμα ἐπὶ τὴν προκειμένην αὐτῷ ὑγίειαν. ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐκ ἤκουσαν ὅλου τοῦ „αὐτὸς γὰρ ἀλγεῖν ποιεῖ καὶ πάλιν ἀποκαθίστησιν“ ἀλλὰ μόνου τοῦ „ἀλγεῖν ποιεῖ.“ οὕτω τοίνυν καὶ ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος ἐκτεθειμένος τὸ „ὦ πάτερ, εἴθε δύναιτο τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο παρελθεῖν,“ οὐκέτι δὲ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς καὶ τὰ παριστάντα τὴν Ἰησοῦ πρὸς τὸ πάθος παρασκευὴν καὶ εὐτονίαν. καὶ ταῦτα δὲ, πολλὴν ἔχοντα διήγησιν ἀπὸ σοφίας θεοῦ οἷς ὁ Παῦλος ὠνόμασε „τελείοις“ εὐλόγως παραδοθησομένην. λέγων· „σοφίαν δὲ λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις.“ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος ὑπερτιθέμενοι ἐπ᾿ ὀλίγον ὑπομιμνησκόμεθα τῶν πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον χρησίμων.
pass_a_gloss: Next after these, wishing (θέλων) to establish (παραστῆσαι) that the things that happened (συμβάντα) to him were painful (ἀλγεινά) and grievous (ἀνιαρά), and that it was not possible (οὐχ οἷόν τε) for him, having willed (βουληθέντα), to make them not such, he says: 'Why then does he wail/cry piteously (ποτνιᾶται) and lament (ὀδύρεται) and pray (εὔχεται) to run past/escape (παραδραμεῖν) the fear (φόβος) of destruction/death (ὄλεθρος), saying somewhat thus: O Father, if this cup (ποτήριον) can pass by (παρελθεῖν)?' And in these see the villainy/malice (κακοῦργον) of Celsus: that not accepting (ἀποδεξάμενος) the truth-loving (φιλάληθες) of those who wrote down (ἀναγράψαντες) the Gospels, who were able to pass over in silence (παρασιωπῆσαι) the things which, as Celsus thinks, are blameworthy (ἔγκλητα), but did not keep silent for many reasons (λόγοι) which someone will give in due time (ἐν καιρῷ) expounding (διηγούμενος) the Gospel, he accuses (κατηγορεῖ) the Gospel wording (λέξις), tragically exaggerating besides (προσεκτραγῳδῶν) and setting down things not written; for it is not found how Jesus laments. And he paraphrases (παραφράζει) 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass,' but no longer cites (παρατίθεται) what straightway displays (ἐμφαῖνον) his piety (εὐσέβεια) toward the Father and greatness of soul (μεγαλοψυχία), written next after it, running thus: 'Yet not as I will, but as you.' Nor does he pretend/profess (προσποιεῖται) to have read the ready obedience (εὐπείθεια) of Jesus to the will (βούλημα) of the Father concerning the things decided (κεκριμένα) that he should suffer, shown in 'If this cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will (θέλημα) be done.' Doing something like the impious (ἀσεβεῖς) who hear the divine writings (θεῖαι γραφαί) more maliciously and speak 'injustice (ἀδικία) unto the height (ὕψος).' For they seem to have heard 'I will kill (ἀποκτενῶ)' and often reproach (ὀνειδίζουσι) us with it, but of 'I will make live (ζῆν ποιήσω)' they do not even remember; the whole saying (ῥητόν) showing that those living for common harm (ἐπὶ κοινῷ κακῷ) and acting according to wickedness (κακία) are killed by God, and a better life (ζωή κρείττων) is brought in in exchange (ἀντεισάγεσθαι) for them, which God would give to those who have died to sin (ἁμαρτία). So they heard 'I will strike (πατάξω)' but no longer see 'and I will heal (ἰάσομαι)'; which is like something said by a physician (ἰατρός) who has cut (διελόντος) bodies and made severe wounds (τραύματα) in order to remove what harms and hinders health (ὑγίεια), and does not end (καταλήξαντος) at the pains and the cutting (διαίρεσις) but restores (ἀποκαθιστῶντος) by treatment (θεραπεία) the body to the health proposed for it. But they did not hear the whole of 'For he makes to feel pain (ἀλγεῖν ποιεῖ) and again restores (ἀποκαθίστησιν),' but only 'makes to feel pain.' So then the Jew set forth in Celsus, having set out 'O Father, would that (εἴθε) this cup could pass,' [set out] no longer the following words and those showing (παριστάντα) Jesus' preparation (παρασκευή) and vigour/firmness (εὐτονία) toward the passion (πάθος). And these things, having much exposition (διήγησις) from the wisdom (σοφία) of God, fittingly (εὐλόγως) to be handed down (παραδοθησομένην) to those whom Paul named 'perfect/mature (τέλειοι),' saying 'But we speak wisdom among the perfect,' postponing (ὑπερτιθέμενοι) for the present, for a little we remind ourselves (ὑπομιμνησκόμεθα) of what is useful to the matter proposed.
pass_b_english: Next, wishing to show that what happened to him was painful and grievous, and that even if he willed it he could not make it otherwise, he says: “Why then does he wail and lament, and pray to escape the fear of death, saying something like this: ‘O Father, if this cup can pass by’ (Matthew 26:39)?”

Here too observe Celsus’s malice. He does not credit the love of truth shown by those who wrote the Gospels. They could have passed over in silence the things that Celsus thinks discreditable, yet they did not keep silent, for many reasons, which someone will give in due time when expounding the Gospel. Instead he attacks the wording of the Gospel, piling tragic exaggeration on top of it and putting down what is not written; for nowhere is Jesus found lamenting. He paraphrases “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass” (Matthew 26:39), but he does not go on to quote what is recorded immediately after it, which at once shows Jesus’ reverence toward the Father and his greatness of soul. It runs: “Yet not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). Nor does he let on that he has read of Jesus’ ready obedience to the Father’s will concerning what had been decided that he should suffer, made plain in the words: “If this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (Matthew 26:42).

In this he acts much like the impious, who listen to the divine Scriptures with malice and “speak injustice on high” (Psalm 73:8). For they too seem to have heard “I will kill,” and they often throw it in our faces, but “I will make alive” (Deuteronomy 32:39) they do not even remember. Yet the whole saying shows that those who live to the common harm and act out of wickedness are put to death by God, and that a better life is brought in for them in its place, the life God would give to those who have died to sin (Romans 6:2). In the same way they have heard “I will strike,” but they do not go on to see “and I will heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39). That is like what a physician might say who has cut into bodies and made severe wounds in order to remove what harms them and stands in the way of health, and who does not stop at the pain and the cutting but by his treatment restores the body to the health he intended for it. Nor have they heard the whole of “For he causes pain, and restores again” (Job 5:18), but only “he causes pain.”

So too, then, Celsus’s Jew has set out “O Father, would that this cup could pass by” (Matthew 26:39), but not what follows, nor what shows Jesus’ readiness and firmness in facing his passion. These matters call for a long explanation drawn from the wisdom of God, which will fittingly be handed on to those whom Paul called “mature,” when he says: “Yet among the mature we speak wisdom” (1 Corinthians 2:6). Setting them aside for the present, we shall briefly recall what is useful for the question before us.

choices.why: βουληθέντα: 'by an act of will' -> 'even if he willed it' (concessive aorist participle)
restored dropped connective καὶ γὰρ: 'For they too seem to have heard'
οὐκέτι δὲ ὁρῶσι: calque 'no longer see' -> 'do not go on to see'
παραδοθησομένην is future: 'may fittingly be handed on' -> 'will fittingly be handed on'; 'admit of' -> 'call for'
ἐπ᾿ ὀλίγον ὑπομιμνησκόμεθα: 'for a little while recall' -> 'briefly recall'

translator_notes: Speaker: ‘he says’ (λέγει) continues from 2.23, where Celsus’s Jew is speaking; kept as the Greek frames it. Celsus’s quoted question is in double quotation marks; his citation of the Gospel inside it is in single marks. Celsus’s two forms of the prayer differ from the Gospel text and from each other (‘εἰ δύναται... παρελθεῖν’, later ‘εἴθε δύναιτο... παρελθεῖν’); both rendered as given and cited to Matthew 26:39 (closest wording; compare Mark 14:36, Luke 22:42). ‘ὀλέθρου’ rendered ‘death’ (lit. destruction). ‘ἀδικίαν εἰς τὸ ὕψος’ = LXX Psalm 72:8, English Psalm 73:8 (Hebrew-based English versions differ in wording). Deuteronomy 32:39 supplies both ‘I will kill... I will make alive’ and ‘I will strike, and I will heal’. ‘those who have died to sin’ is a clear verbal echo of Romans 6:2 (compare 6:11). ‘αὐτὸς γὰρ ἀλγεῖν ποιεῖ καὶ πάλιν ἀποκαθίστησιν’ = LXX Job 5:18. ‘τελείοις’ rendered ‘mature’ to match the 1 Corinthians 2:6 citation. The edition’s punctuation has stray full stops mid-clause (e.g. ‘ὦ πάτερ. εἰ’); read through them. ‘προσποιεῖται ἀνεγνωκέναι’ (he does not make a show of having read) rendered ‘nor does he let on that he has read’.
